visuals.title: Quiz
visuals.text: Five questions. Answer along on the cards below the transcript, then hear Marco's answers.

quiz.pause_at: Pause here if you want to think it through

questions.q: A DCF gives an enterprise value of 800m. Net debt is 200m. There are 40m basic shares and 50m diluted shares. What's a share worth?
questions.explain: Subtract net debt first: 800 − 200 = 600m of equity. Then divide by the diluted count: 600 ÷ 50 = 12. Dividing enterprise value by shares gives 16; using basic shares gives 15.
questions.explain_at: Two mistakes. Enterprise value belongs to lenders and shareholders together

questions.q: In a DCF sensitivity table, why does the high corner sit further from the middle than the low corner?

options.text: Higher growth also raises the forecast years
The rate-minus-growth gap is a denominator
Low discount rates are more common in practice
Bankers set wider ranges on the upside

questions.explain: Terminal value divides by the discount rate minus growth. Shrinking that gap from 7 points to 5 raises value more than widening it to 9 lowers it.
questions.explain_at: Because the gap between the discount rate and the growth rate sits at the bottom of a fraction

questions.q: You raise the growth rate in your forecast and leave capex unchanged. What's the problem?

options.text: It's fine: growth and capex are separate inputs
The discount rate should fall to match
The tax rate should rise with the profits
Growth comes free, so value is overstated

questions.explain: Growth needs reinvestment: new sites, equipment, working capital. Good models link the growth rate to capex, so faster growth means less free cash flow in the early years.

questions.q: What went wrong in Tibco's 2014 sale to Vista Equity Partners?

options.text: The growth rate was set too high
Net debt was left out of the bridge
Staff options were left out of the count

questions.explain: About 4.1 million unvested restricted shares were double-counted, so $24 a share added up to about $100m less than the equity value the deal was presented at.
questions.explain_at: counted about four point one million unvested restricted shares twice

options.text: A DCF run at the buyer's discount rate
A DCF built on the seller's own forecast
Working out what growth a price requires
Building a DCF, then comparing it to the price

questions.explain: You start from the price paid and solve for the growth and margins it implies, then judge whether they're believable. Comparing one model with the price gives a verdict, not a test.
questions.explain_at: That's a reverse D-C-F: start from the price
